facts.text: Many states require a separate braking system on trailers with a loaded weight of more than 1,500 pounds; Ford recommends a separate functional brake system on any towed vehicle, including dolly-towed or towbar-towed.

Trailer brake types described: electronically controlled brakes, electric-over-hydraulic (EOH) brakes (many compatible with the factory Trailer Brake Controller), and surge brakes; surge-brake hydraulics must never be connected to the tow vehicle's hydraulic system.
Do not tow a trailer until the vehicle has been driven at least 1,000 miles.
Always use safety chains, crossed under the trailer tongue, with only enough slack to permit full turning.
Base Curb Weight is the vehicle with a full tank of fuel and all standard equipment, without passengers, cargo or optional equipment.
Cargo Weight includes all weight added to Base Curb Weight, including optional equipment; trailer tongue load or king pin weight is part of Cargo Weight.
Payload is the combined maximum allowable weight of cargo and passengers: GVWR minus Base Curb Weight.
GVWR (Gross Vehicle Weight Rating) is the maximum allowable weight of the fully loaded vehicle, shown on the Safety Compliance Certification Label; GVW must never exceed GVWR.
GAWR (Gross Axle Weight Rating) is the maximum weight to be carried by a single axle; the load on each axle must never exceed its GAWR.
GCWR (Gross Combination Weight Rating) is the maximum allowable weight of the towing vehicle and loaded trailer, including all cargo and passengers; the measured GCW must never exceed GCWR.
The towing vehicle's brake system is rated for operation at the GVWR, not GCWR; separate functional brakes should be used for trailers weighing more than 1,500 lbs. loaded.

Maximum Loaded Trailer Weight assumes minimum towing vehicle GVW with mandatory options, no cargo, tongue load of 10% (conventional) or king pin weight of 15% (5th-wheel), and a driver and passenger of 150 lbs. each; additional options, passengers, cargo and hitch weight must be deducted.
Tongue load: for trailers up to 2,000 lbs., not to exceed 200 lbs.; for conventional trailers over 2,000 lbs., 10% of loaded trailer weight; 5th-wheel king pin weight is 15% of loaded trailer weight.
Examples: a 5,000-lb. conventional trailer needs a 500-lb. tongue load; an 11,500-lb. 5th-wheel trailer gives a 1,725-lb. king pin weight.
Tongue load or king pin weight must not cause GVWR or rear GAWR to be exceeded.

Weight distribution correction factor: 50% for Expedition, F-150, F-150 Lightning, F-150 Raptor, F-250/F-350 Super Duty and Super Duty Chassis Cab; F-450 pickup 25% Regular Cab, 50% Crew Cab; not required for Explorer, Maverick, Ranger, Bronco, Bronco Sport, Escape, Mustang; Transit use not recommended.
Weight-distributing hitch setup: measure front fender lip height unhitched (H1) and hitched without bars (H2); target height = H2 minus (H2 - H1) x correction factor.
Approximately 60% of the allowable cargo weight should be in the front half of the trailer and 40% in the rear, within tongue load or king pin limits.
At high altitude, reduce GVW and GCW by 2% per 1,000 ft. of elevation.
A conventional, identical full-size spare tire is required for trailer towing.
The charts show the minimum powertrain needed for acceptable towing performance at the listed GCW; large frontal area or hilly terrain may call for a higher rating.
Tow capability could be reduced based on the weight of the selected trim series and option content.
